sentences.sentence: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said on Oct 12 that small AI models "may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes"
The post, by William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, reports the company's own evaluations
Every result below is Anthropic's claim, and its key replication test was, in Anthropic's word, "simplified"
Anthropic splits the job into four stages: finding targets, gaining access to run code, getting a model running and spreading further
Its tests focused on getting a model running and largely set the hacking stages aside
sentences.dossier: dossier-news.md section 2: Anthropic 'largely ignore[s] the cyber exploit element'

sentences.sentence: Models of 30 billion parameters and under ... can already do many single steps but "make mistakes when composing them end to end"
sentences.note: Definition of parameters is the writer's gloss.

sentences.sentence: a 9-billion-parameter model "got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested"
Tom's Hardware names the model as Qwen3.5-9B and says the hardware ranged from Nvidia Jetson Nano devices to Apple Silicon Macs and at least one PC with an RTX 4090
Anthropic built a walled-off network of 8 cloud computers running an Android 15 emulator
sentences.note: 'firewalled VPC of 8 GCP nodes running redroid'; cloud vendor name omitted.

sentences.sentence: The worm had to hop from node to node through an ADB port that required no login and set up a Llama 3.1 8B model on each
sentences.dossier: Llama3.1-8B payload: dossier-news.md section 2; also n18

sentences.sentence: Only GLM-5.2 did it reliably. It reached all 8 nodes in 4 of 5 trials and 7 of 8 in the other, while the other models "fail reliably"
Anthropic kept the hacking step trivial and calls the result "an upper bound on real-world success"
Tom's Hardware notes that it ran on a separate server and set up "the much smaller Llama 3.1 8B" on each target
successive copies of Qwen3.5-9B passed notes forward, which lifted setup success from 45% to between 61% and 84%
eWeek points out that those copies "were restarted by the researchers rather than reproducing autonomously"
Advice from a stronger frontier model, Opus 4.8, did not measurably help
Anthropic ran one model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, split across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes that cost about $55 each
It produced 0.39 tokens, or word pieces, per second
That was a test of running a model on cheap hardware, not a replication.
sentences.dossier: dossier-news.md section 1 and 'Press error to avoid'; caller caveat (2)

sentences.sentence: if small models keep improving at their historical rate, "they'll match this capability level by the end of this year"
That forecast rests on a general capability index rising 13.7 points a year, which Anthropic calls "only a rough estimate"

Each 9B copy takes over 1 to 2 days, and a swarm the size of the Kimwolf botnet ... would have "at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference," which Anthropic calls "a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms"
Tom's Hardware estimates that infecting 2 million devices would take about 6,300 agent-years, and notes that real-world security controls were not tested
"The threat is real, but still in the future, at least for now," its subheading says
sentences.dossier: dossier-news.md Quotable lines #3; fact-check confirmed it is the standfirst/subheading

sentences.sentence: An early comment on a Hacker News thread (106 points, 109 comments when checked) called the post "fearmarketing," while granting "there does seem to be a cool technical demo here"
sentences.note: Counts per fact-check; comment is by pythonaut_16, not the top comment.

sentences.sentence: Other commenters doubted the year-end projection for small models
"We don't yet have a full rogue replicator," the post says
A replicator spreading at scale would leave a network signature that traffic monitoring could flag
sentences.note: ISP reference in the source quote deliberately omitted.

sentences.sentence: "We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay"
Telling a reasoning model to skip its thinking often fails, according to a preprint posted to arXiv on Oct 8 by Dianqiao Lei, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Pan Lu, Philip Torr and James Zou
With thinking switched off, DeepSeek-V4-Flash still wrote out visible reasoning in 99.9% of open-ended answers
The arXiv version is a preprint.
The authors, from Tsinghua University, the University of Oxford and Stanford University, say it has been accepted to NeurIPS 2026, in both the arXiv comments field and the project README
sentences.note: Attributed to the authors. arXiv comments field ('Accepted by NeurIPS 2026') per fact-check.

sentences.sentence: Reasoning models write out step-by-step working before they answer, and many now come with a switch to turn that off.
The authors found that "explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible inference"
They call the effect "Thinking Inertia," and it grows "as the answer space opens"
With thinking off, most models gave answer-only replies 80% to 100% of the time on yes/no questions, but almost never on open-ended ones
GPT-5.4 was the main exception when a step-by-step prompt was added: it stayed answer-only on yes/no and multiple-choice questions where other models resumed reasoning
The team tested six prompt settings, from thinking switched on to a strict demand for a bare answer, on six models
three sizes of Qwen3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3-Flash
Questions came from six benchmarks, from yes/no sets like BoolQ to math sets like GSM8K and MATH, for 572,688 outputs in all

A GPT-5.5 judge flagged whether the text before each answer held a real reasoning step. On 600 outputs checked by people, the human labels agreed with that judge 98.8% of the time and with a second judge, Claude Opus 4.8, 96.7% of the time
On open-ended tasks, a strict "answer directly" prompt raised the answer-only rate from near zero to about 40%, but cut accuracy by about 15 percentage points
Pre-filling the reply with "The answer is" did not reliably work either
When the same multiple-choice questions were rewritten as yes/no for Qwen3-32B, answer-only replies rose from 10.5% to 62.5%, while accuracy held at 77.8% versus 78.9%
The paper warns that "stopping explicit reasoning cannot be assumed from model settings or instructions alone"
sentences.dossier: dossier-research.md Quotable lines #2; fact-check found it in the full-text introduction, so cited to [6]

sentences.sentence: The authors suggest "task-aware routing": answer directly when the question gives enough support, and keep the reasoning when cutting it would cost accuracy
"Knowing when NOT to think may be just as important as knowing how to think," the first author wrote on Hugging Face
A 2025 survey already noted that "Zhu et al. (2025a) find that LRMs do not always follow the instruction to skip thinking," where LRMs are large reasoning models
This paper adds a way to measure it and the link to answer format.
The study also looks only at visible text, not hidden computation, cost or speed
"Visible compliance should not, however, be equated with lower inference cost when hidden reasoning may remain active"
visible reasoning does not always reflect a model's actual process
skipping thinking by prompt "can be surprisingly effective"
One Hugging Face commenter was blunter: "if you train a model to think, it'll think"
The authors list code, tool use, other languages and multi-turn chats as untested, and want to train models for "calibrated stopping rather than uniform suppression"
Plimsoll runs untrusted code, such as code an AI agent wrote, inside a sandbox, and "every result says how strong that sandbox was"
A request can demand a minimum strength: "if the sandbox is weaker, nothing runs"
Its author shared the open-source project on Hacker News on Oct 11
The name comes from the Plimsoll line, the load limit painted on a ship's hull. Strength comes in four tiers, weakest first: process, container, kernel and vm
Plimsoll doesn't build the walls. It hands that job to gVisor and Firecracker and acts as the gatekeeper in front of them
gVisor "intercepts application system calls and acts as the guest kernel," the basis of the kernel tier
Table row 1: Kernel tier; a TypeScript compile-and-run took 4.1 s vs 1.95 s in a plain container, in the author's test
Table rows 1-2: Says which wall you got: Yes, on every result
Table rows 1-2: Refuses runs below a minimum: Yes, if the request sets a floor
Table row 2: VM tier, billed by the second
Table row 2: Yes, but inferred from which provider is configured
Table row 3: Can vary by host; Northflank uses gVisor "where nested virtualisation is unavailable"
Table row 3: No, per the author (reports tier / refuses below minimum)
The idea came from a JavaScript sandbox that "advertised a MemoryLimit that did nothing," the author writes
In tests on one laptop, the author found that Docker accepted a 64-process limit under the Kata runtime, yet 200 of 200 processes started
The author says a Kata issue about the limit not reaching the guest, opened in 2022, was closed as not planned
sentences.note: [21] supports the issue's existence and 2022 opening; 'closed as not planned' is attributed to the author's note [20] because issue state was unverifiable.

sentences.sentence: The README says the tier "is not attestation, cryptographic proof from the hardware of what software is running"
A compromised Docker daemon or E2B control plane "defeats the evidence," the security notes add
The per-request floor is also opt-in, so a request that sets none skips the check
The project is "pre-1.0, single author, no external users yet," and has had no third-party security audit
As the author put it, "the bus factor is one"

All three stories ask whether AI stays inside the limits people set for it. Reasoning models keep thinking after being told to stop. Anthropic says small models can already set themselves up on new hardware, and Plimsoll refuses to run agent code when the request demands a stronger wall than it can provide.
